aeo.what_is: Severe mood and physical symptoms occurring before menstruation that significantly disrupt work, relationships, and daily life each month.

content.temporal_criteria: Symptoms must occur during the luteal phase (week before menstruation) in the majority of menstrual cycles, start to improve within a few days after menses onset, and become minimal or absent in the week postmenses. Diagnosis requires prospective daily tracking for at least two symptomatic cycles to confirm the cyclical pattern.

confused_with: Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS) — PMS involves milder premenstrual symptoms that don't severely impair functioning. PMDD requires at least five symptoms (including one core mood symptom) with marked distress or functional impairment.

Major Depressive Disorder or Bipolar Disorder — if mood symptoms occur throughout the month (not just luteal phase), it may be a primary mood disorder. Some people have both PMDD and a mood disorder, where premenstrual worsening occurs on top of baseline symptoms.
Generalized Anxiety Disorder — GAD involves chronic anxiety not tied to the menstrual cycle. PMDD anxiety is cyclical and resolves after menses.
Thyroid Disorders or Perimenopause — thyroid dysfunction and perimenopausal hormone changes can cause mood and energy symptoms. Labs and cycle tracking help distinguish.
Irritable Bowel Syndrome — IBS can worsen premenstrually, causing bloating and discomfort, but PMDD includes prominent mood symptoms (irritability, depression, anxiety) as the core feature.
misdiagnosis_explained.clarifying_factors: Prospective daily symptom tracking (Daily Record of Severity of Problems, DRSP) for two or more cycles to confirm symptoms appear in luteal phase and resolve after menses; ruling out other mood, anxiety, or medical conditions; assessing functional impairment (missing work/school, relationship conflicts); confirming symptoms are not just an exacerbation of another disorder.
misdiagnosis_explained.timeline_differences: Primary mood/anxiety disorders have symptoms throughout the month. PMDD symptoms appear only in the luteal phase (typically the week before menstruation) and resolve within days of bleeding. PMS symptoms are milder and less impairing.
misdiagnosis_explained.impairment_differences: PMS causes discomfort but people usually function. PMDD causes significant impairment—missing work, severe relationship conflict, inability to manage daily tasks. Primary mood disorders cause chronic impairment, while PMDD is cyclical.

description.overview: Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD) is a severe form of premenstrual syndrome characterized by marked mood, behavioral, and physical symptoms that occur during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle and resolve shortly after menses onset. The symptoms cause significant distress or functional impairment and are cyclical in nature.
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life: A 29-year-old nurse notices that the week before her period, she becomes intensely irritable, snaps at coworkers and family, cries easily, and feels overwhelmed. The day her period starts, it's like a switch flips and she feels 'normal' again. This pattern repeats every month.

A 32-year-old can predict her period down to the day because exactly one week before, she feels crushing anxiety, hopelessness, and physical bloating. She calls in sick to work, avoids social events, and fights with her partner. When her period arrives, the cloud lifts.

A 26-year-old tracks her mood and realizes that every month, she has a 'bad week' where she feels depressed, exhausted, and has no interest in activities she usually enjoys. She thought she was just moody until she connected it to her cycle.

A 35-year-old teacher has to plan her life around her cycle. The week before her period, she experiences severe mood swings, tension, and joint pain. She avoids scheduling important meetings or social events during this time because she knows she won't be able to cope.

A 40-year-old experiences such severe premenstrual anger and irritability that her family has learned to give her space. She feels out of control, saying things she regrets. When her period starts, she feels guilty about how she acted but knows it will happen again next month.

A 27-year-old has suicidal thoughts only during the week before her period. The rest of the month, she's fine. Her therapist initially diagnosed depression until prospective tracking revealed the clear cyclical pattern, leading to a PMDD diagnosis.
common_reactions_to_diagnosis: Relief that the cyclical mood changes have a name and aren't 'just PMS' or personal weakness.
Validation that the severity of symptoms is real and not exaggerated.
Frustration that it's been dismissed as normal premenstrual changes for years.
Hope that treatment can bring stability throughout the month.
Sadness about losing one week of every month to severe symptoms.
Anger that a hormonal condition can so profoundly affect mood and functioning.
Empowerment from understanding the pattern and being able to plan and treat it.

content.diagnostic_criteria: A. In the majority of menstrual cycles, at least five symptoms must be present in the final week before menses, start to improve within a few days after onset of menses, and become minimal or absent in the week postmenses. B. One or more of the following must be present: marked affective lability, irritability/anger/increased interpersonal conflicts, depressed mood/hopelessness/self-deprecating thoughts, anxiety/tension/keyed-up feelings. C. One or more of the following must additionally be present to reach a total of five symptoms when combined with Criterion B: decreased interest in usual activities, difficulty concentrating, lethargy/easy fatigability, marked change in appetite, hypersomnia or insomnia, sense of being overwhelmed or out of control, physical symptoms (e.g., breast tenderness, joint/muscle pain, bloating, weight gain). D. Symptoms are associated with clinically significant distress or interference. E. Not merely an exacerbation of another disorder. F. Criterion A should be confirmed by prospective daily ratings for at least two symptomatic cycles. G. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition.
content.prevalence: Estimated to affect 1–5% of menstruating individuals; more common in the late 20s to mid-40s age range.
content.age_of_onset: Typically emerges in the 20s to 30s, after ovulatory cycles are established; may worsen toward perimenopause.
content.prognosis: Chronic cyclic course until menopause unless treated; many improve significantly with SSRIs, hormonal therapy, or combined approaches. Prognosis is excellent with targeted treatment and lifestyle support.

circuitry: Heightened sensitivity of limbic structures (amygdala, anterior cingulate) to normal hormonal fluctuations.
Altered prefrontal-limbic connectivity impacting emotional regulation during the luteal phase.
neurochemistry: Normal estrogen and progesterone levels, but abnormal central nervous system sensitivity to neuroactive steroid metabolites (e.g., allopregnanolone) that modulate GABA-A receptors.
Altered serotonergic transmission in luteal phase contributes to mood and irritability symptoms.
neurobiology.genetic_environmental: Familial aggregation suggests heritable sensitivity to hormonal changes; stress and trauma may exacerbate symptom severity.

history_psychosocial: Detailed menstrual history including cycle length, ovulation patterns, and symptom timing in relation to menses.
Mood, anxiety, irritability, and physical symptom patterns; functional impact on work, school, and relationships.
History of mood or anxiety disorders; family psychiatric and gynecologic history.
medical_assessment: Physical and gynecologic exam as indicated.
Rule out thyroid dysfunction, anemia, and perimenopausal changes.
standardized_measures: Prospective symptom charting with Daily Record of Severity of Problems (DRSP) or similar for at least two cycles.
risk_stratification: Assess impact on safety (e.g., self-harm during luteal phase), work, and relationships.
Evaluate comorbid depression, anxiety, or substance use.
differential_diagnosis: Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS) – fewer symptoms, less severity, no marked impairment.
Exacerbation of another mood or anxiety disorder.
Bipolar disorder with cyclical mood changes.
evaluation.team_and_process: Collaborative care between gynecology and mental health providers; involve primary care for comorbidity management.

core: Loss of interest in usual activities
Physical symptoms such as bloating, breast tenderness, or joint pain

severity_levels.mild: Symptoms noticeable but do not significantly impair functioning.
severity_levels.moderate: Symptoms cause difficulty in work, school, or relationships but remain manageable.
severity_levels.severe: Marked impairment in multiple domains; risk of self-harm or severe interpersonal conflict.

psychological: History of depression, anxiety, or trauma

impact_on_life.school_work: Missed work or school days; reduced productivity and concentration.
impact_on_life.social: Interpersonal conflicts and withdrawal during luteal phase.
impact_on_life.medical: Increased use of healthcare resources for symptom relief.
impact_on_life.emotional: Recurrent mood instability leading to frustration and distress.

psychotherapy: CBT targeting mood regulation, stress management, and coping with cyclical changes.
Interpersonal therapy to address relationship stressors.
medications: SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine) – can be given continuously or luteal phase only.
SNRIs (venlafaxine) for those unresponsive to SSRIs.
Combined oral contraceptives (e.g., drospirenone-containing) to suppress ovulation.
GnRH agonists for refractory cases, with add-back hormone therapy to mitigate bone loss.
lifestyle_interventions: Balanced diet rich in complex carbohydrates, calcium, and vitamin B6.
Limit caffeine, alcohol, and salt during luteal phase.
Sleep hygiene and stress reduction techniques.
supplements: Chasteberry extract (Vitex agnus-castus) – limited evidence but may help some
care_coordination: Cycle tracking with both patient and provider input.
Collaboration between gynecology, psychiatry, and primary care.

treatment_goals: Reduce or eliminate cyclical mood and physical symptoms.
Improve functioning and quality of life across the menstrual cycle.
missed_diagnosis_factors: Symptoms dismissed as normal PMS without prospective tracking.
Overlap with other mood disorders masking cyclical nature.
Failure to link symptom onset/resolution with menstrual phases.
overdiagnosis_factors: Labeling PMS or situational stress as PMDD without meeting full criteria.
Misinterpretation of mood symptoms from primary mood disorder as PMDD.

pattern: Confirmed with prospective daily ratings for at least two cycles

warning_signs: Emergence of suicidal thoughts during luteal phase.
Severe functional impairment or absenteeism each cycle.
self_help_strategies: Track symptoms daily to anticipate onset and plan coping strategies.
Schedule demanding tasks outside the luteal phase when possible.
Practice relaxation and mindfulness exercises regularly.

adolescence: May present as severe PMS with mood swings and irritability impacting school performance; often underrecognized.
adulthood: Cyclic mood instability and physical symptoms disrupting work and relationships; peak severity often in 30s.
perimenopause: Fluctuating cycle lengths and hormone levels may intensify symptoms before eventual resolution at menopause.

first_person_statements: I felt like Jekyll and Hyde—half the month I was fine, and then I'd turn into someone I didn't recognize for a week before my period.
I used to think I was losing my mind. Then I started tracking my symptoms and realized it was always the same week of my cycle.
People would tell me 'it's just PMS, everyone gets it,' but this was debilitating. I couldn't work, couldn't function, couldn't control my emotions.
The hopelessness during that week was so intense I had suicidal thoughts. But the day my period started, it lifted. That's when I knew something was really wrong.
Treatment changed my life. I didn't realize how much of my month I was losing to PMDD until I got it under control.
My partner learned to recognize the signs before I did. They'd gently suggest I check my cycle when I started getting irritable, and sure enough, it was always the same time.

comparisons: It's like a monthly storm that rolls in with dark clouds, heavy rain, and chaos, and then clears completely once your period arrives, leaving you wondering how you survived it.

Imagine your brain chemistry shifts dramatically for one week every month, making everything harder—controlling emotions, concentrating, coping with stress—and then resets as soon as you start bleeding.
Think of it as a switch that flips between 'functional' and 'barely hanging on,' tied directly to your hormonal cycle, with no middle ground.
It's like living with two different versions of yourself: one who can handle life, and one who's overwhelmed, irritable, and hopeless—and you never know which one will show up each week.

faqs.question: How is PMDD different from regular PMS?
faqs.answer: PMDD is much more severe. PMS may cause mild irritability, bloating, or fatigue, but PMDD involves severe mood symptoms (depression, anxiety, anger) that significantly impair work, relationships, and daily functioning. PMDD requires at least five symptoms and marked distress or impairment.

faqs.question: Can PMDD be cured?
faqs.answer: PMDD can't be 'cured,' but it can be very effectively managed with treatment (SSRIs, hormonal therapies, lifestyle changes). Many people achieve near-complete symptom relief. PMDD typically resolves at menopause when ovulation stops.

faqs.question: Do I need to track my symptoms to get diagnosed?
faqs.answer: Yes. Diagnosis requires prospective daily symptom tracking for at least two menstrual cycles to confirm that symptoms occur in the luteal phase and resolve after menses. Retrospective recall alone is not sufficient.

faqs.question: Can antidepressants help if PMDD is hormonal?
faqs.answer: Yes. SSRIs are first-line treatment for PMDD. Even though PMDD is hormonally triggered, the mood symptoms involve serotonin dysregulation. SSRIs can be taken continuously or just during the luteal phase, and both approaches work well.

faqs.question: Will birth control help PMDD?
faqs.answer: Some birth control pills help PMDD, especially those containing drospirenone (like Yaz), which suppress ovulation. However, some people find hormonal contraceptives worsen mood. It varies by individual, so close monitoring is needed.

faqs.question: What if I have suicidal thoughts only before my period?
faqs.answer: This is a serious symptom of PMDD and requires immediate treatment. SSRIs, hormonal therapy, and close psychiatric monitoring can help. If you have suicidal thoughts, contact your doctor, go to an ER, or call 988.

faqs.question: Can PMDD affect my relationships?
faqs.answer: Yes. The irritability, mood swings, and withdrawal during the luteal phase can strain relationships. Many partners and family members learn to recognize the pattern. Psychoeducation for loved ones and couple's therapy can help.

faqs.question: What if I have PMDD and another mood disorder?
faqs.answer: You can have both. Some people have baseline depression or anxiety that worsens premenstrually (premenstrual exacerbation) or have both PMDD and a separate mood disorder. Treatment often requires addressing both conditions.

faqs.question: Can exercise and diet help PMDD?
faqs.answer: Yes. Regular aerobic exercise, reducing caffeine and salt, eating balanced meals with complex carbs, and supplements (calcium, vitamin B6) can reduce symptoms. However, lifestyle changes alone are usually not sufficient for moderate to severe PMDD.

faqs.question: How common is PMDD?
faqs.answer: PMDD affects about 3–8% of menstruating individuals. It's less common than PMS but significantly more impairing.

faqs.question: Will PMDD go away after having children?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Some people report improvement after pregnancy, others worsen, and many have no change. Postpartum hormonal shifts can be unpredictable for people with PMDD.

faqs.question: Can I take medication only during the luteal phase?
faqs.answer: Yes. Luteal-phase dosing (taking SSRIs only during the week or two before your period) is effective for many people with PMDD and can reduce overall medication exposure.

faqs.question: What if hormonal treatments don't work?
faqs.answer: If SSRIs and hormonal therapies fail, GnRH agonists (which create a temporary menopause-like state) can be used with add-back hormones. In very severe, treatment-resistant cases, some people consider surgical menopause (hysterectomy with oophorectomy), but this is a last resort.

faqs.question: Is PMDD recognized as a real disorder?
faqs.answer: Yes. PMDD is included in the DSM-5 as a distinct depressive disorder. It's recognized by medical and psychiatric communities as a serious condition requiring treatment.

faqs.question: Will PMDD symptoms change as I get older?
faqs.answer: PMDD may worsen in the years leading up to menopause (perimenopause) due to erratic hormone fluctuations. After menopause, when ovulation stops, PMDD typically resolves.

real_life_examples.person: A 29-year-old nurse noticed intense irritability, tearfulness, and bloating the week before her period, resolving within two days of bleeding. Daily tracking with the DRSP confirmed PMDD. Her doctor started luteal-phase sertraline (taken only during the premenstrual week). Combined with yoga and limiting caffeine, her symptoms reduced by 80%, and she no longer calls in sick or fights with her partner.

A 35-year-old teacher experienced disabling fatigue, anxiety, and conflict with colleagues premenstrually. She started a drospirenone-containing birth control pill, which suppressed ovulation and stabilized her mood. CBT helped her manage residual stress and anticipate her cycle. Her work attendance and relationships improved dramatically.

A 27-year-old with severe premenstrual depression and suicidal ideation tried SSRIs continuously without much benefit. Her psychiatrist switched her to a GnRH agonist with estrogen/progesterone add-back therapy, creating a stable hormonal state. Her mood stabilized completely, and she's maintained remission for over a year.

A 32-year-old tracked her symptoms for three months and confirmed a clear luteal-phase pattern. She started sertraline taken continuously and added calcium and vitamin B6 supplements. Regular aerobic exercise and reducing salt intake further helped. She described finally feeling 'stable all month' for the first time in years.

A 40-year-old with longstanding PMDD found that hormonal treatments worsened her mood. Her doctor tried continuous high-dose SSRI (escitalopram 20 mg), which provided significant relief. She also worked with a therapist to develop coping strategies for the luteal phase and educated her family about PMDD, which reduced household conflict.

content.when_to_seek_help: Seek help if emotional or physical symptoms before menstruation are severe enough to interfere with daily functioning or relationships, or if suicidal thoughts occur.

positive_factors: Adherence to pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic treatments
challenging_factors: Irregular cycles making symptom timing unclear
